specStatements.text: Acids react with some metals to produce salts and hydrogen.
(HT only) Students should be able to:
explain in terms of gain or loss of electrons, that these are redox reactions
identify which species are oxidised and which are reduced in given chemical equations. Knowledge of reactions limited to those of magnesium, zinc and iron with hydrochloric and sulfuric acids.

Acids are neutralised by alkalis (eg soluble metal hydroxides) and bases (eg insoluble metal hydroxides and metal oxides) to produce salts and water, and by metal carbonates to produce salts, water and carbon dioxide.
The particular salt produced in any reaction between an acid and a base or alkali depends on:
the acid used (hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates, sulfuric acid produces sulfates)
the positive ions in the base, alkali or carbonate.
Students should be able to:
predict products from given reactants
use the formulae of common ions to deduce the formulae of salts.

Soluble salts can be made from acids by reacting them with solid insoluble substances, such as metals, metal oxides, hydroxides or carbonates. The solid is added to the acid until no more reacts and the excess solid is filtered off to produce a solution of the salt.
Salt solutions can be crystallised to produce solid salts.
Students should be able to describe how to make pure, dry samples of named soluble salts from information provided.

Required practical 1: preparation of a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate using a Bunsen burner to heat dilute acid and a water bath or electric heater to evaporate the solution.
Acids produce hydrogen ions (H⁺ ) in aqueous solutions.
Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions (OH⁻ ).
The pH scale, from 0 to 14, is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution, and can be measured using universal indicator or a pH probe.
A solution with pH 7 is neutral. Aqueous solutions of acids have pH values of less than 7 and aqueous solutions of alkalis have pH values greater than 7.
In neutralisation reactions between an acid and an alkali, hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to produce water.
This reaction can be represented by the equation:
Students should be able to:
describe the use of universal indicator or a wide range indicator to measure the approximate pH of a solution
use the pH scale to identify acidic or alkaline solutions.
The volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other can be measured by titration using a suitable indicator.
Students should be able to:
describe how to carry out titrations using strong acids and strong alkalis only (sulfuric, hydrochloric and nitric acids only) to find the reacting volumes accurately
(HT Only) calculate the chemical quantities in titrations involving concentrations in mol/dm³ and in g/dm³ .
Required practical 2: (chemistry only) determination of the reacting volumes of solutions of a strong acid and a strong alkali by titration.
(HT only) determination of the concentration of one of the solutions in mol/dm³ and g/dm³ from the reacting volumes and the known concentration of the other solution.
A strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution. Examples of strong acids are hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids.
A weak acid is only partially ionised in aqueous solution. Examples of weak acids are ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids.
For a given concentration of aqueous solutions, the stronger an acid, the lower the pH.
As the pH decreases by one unit, the hydrogen ion concentration of the solution increases by a factor of 10.
Students should be able to:
use and explain the terms dilute and concentrated (in terms of amount of substance), and weak and strong (in terms of the degree of ionisation) in relation to acids
describe neutrality and relative acidity in terms of the effect on hydrogen ion concentration and the numerical value of pH (whole numbers only).

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of reactions limited to those of magnesium, zinc and iron with hydrochloric and sulfuric acids.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every acid-metal reaction written anywhere in this section is one of magnesium, zinc or iron with hydrochloric or sulfuric acid. The redox analysis is carried out only on those combinations, and iron is always taken to the iron(II) salt that dilute acid actually gives. Copper appears only as a metal that does not react, which is what makes 'some metals' meaningful; no reaction of a metal with nitric acid is set, and no other metal is required to be recalled or balanced.

scopeNotes.statement: describe how to carry out titrations using strong acids and strong alkalis only (sulfuric, hydrochloric and nitric acids only)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every titration in this section uses one of the three named strong acids with a strong alkali, and hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide is the only worked pair. No weak acid is titrated, no weak-acid titration curve is drawn, and no question asks about buffering or a shifting end point, all of which lie outside this boundary.

scopeNotes.statement: Required practical 2: (chemistry only) determination of the reacting volumes of solutions of a strong acid and a strong alkali by titration.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The titration practical is treated as chemistry-only content and is kept to the determination of reacting volumes: apparatus choice, indicator choice and the handling of concordant titres. Nothing in the practical items depends on combined-science-only material.

scopeNotes.statement: describe neutrality and relative acidity in terms of the effect on hydrogen ion concentration and the numerical value of pH (whole numbers only).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every pH value used in this section is a whole number, and every comparison of hydrogen ion concentration is a whole power of ten. No item asks for a logarithm, for [H+] in mol/dm3, or for a pH quoted to a decimal place.

scopeNotes.statement: Required practical 1: ... using a Bunsen burner to heat dilute acid and a water bath or electric heater to evaporate the solution.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The apparatus named in the specification is the apparatus used: a Bunsen burner warms the dilute acid, and the salt solution is evaporated over a water bath or with an electric heater. Direct strong heating of the salt solution appears only as a distractor, and evaporating to dryness is treated as an error rather than a method.

concepts.definition: A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal ion or by another positive ion. The acid supplies the negative ion and the metal, base, alkali or carbonate supplies the positive ion.
Acids react with some metals to produce a salt and hydrogen: for example Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. The hydrogen is seen as bubbles of gas.
Only metals more reactive than hydrogen release hydrogen from a dilute acid. Magnesium, zinc and iron do; copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.
Loss of electrons. When a metal reacts with an acid the metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions, so the metal is oxidised.
Gain of electrons. In an acid-metal reaction the hydrogen ions gain electrons to become hydrogen molecules, so they are reduced.
A reaction in which electrons are transferred, so that oxidation and reduction happen together. Acid-metal reactions are redox reactions.
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, such as Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ or 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
An ion that is present but unchanged by the reaction, such as the chloride ion when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid.
A substance that neutralises an acid to give a salt and water. Insoluble metal hydroxides and metal oxides are bases.
A base that dissolves in water, such as a soluble metal hydroxide. Its aqueous solution contains hydroxide ions.
The reaction of an acid with a base, alkali or carbonate in which the acid is used up and a salt is formed.
Metal carbonates neutralise acids to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide, which is why the mixture fizzes.
The salt's name has two parts: the first comes from the positive ion of the base, alkali or carbonate, the second from the acid used.
Hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates and sulfuric acid produces sulfates.
The positive ion in a salt comes from the base, alkali or carbonate, not from the acid and not from the water formed.
Acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen; acid + base or alkali gives salt + water; acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Familiar ions used to build salt formulae include Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻ and CO₃²⁻.
A salt formula is neutral overall, so the ions are combined in the ratio that cancels the charges, using brackets where a whole ion is repeated, as in Ca(NO₃)₂.
A soluble salt is made by reacting an acid with a solid insoluble metal, metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate, then removing the unreacted solid.
Solid is added until no more reacts, which guarantees that all the acid has been used and none is left to contaminate the salt.
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper. The unreacted solid stays as the residue; the dissolved salt passes through as the filtrate.
Concentrating a salt solution by evaporating some of the water and then leaving it, so that crystals of the solid salt form as the rest evaporates.
Crystals that contain no unreacted acid or solid and no remaining water; they are patted dry between filter papers rather than heated hard.
Preparation of a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate, using a Bunsen burner to heat the dilute acid.
The gentle heating used to evaporate the salt solution in Required practical 1, so that the salt is not decomposed and crystals can form.
The ion that all acids produce in aqueous solution; it is what makes a solution acidic.
The ion present in aqueous solutions of alkalis; it is what makes a solution alkaline.
A scale from 0 to 14 measuring the acidity or alkalinity of a solution, measured with universal indicator or a pH probe.
An instrument that gives a numerical pH reading directly, more precisely than a colour chart can.
A solution with pH 7. Below 7 a solution is acidic, above 7 it is alkaline.
In neutralisation between an acid and an alkali, the hydrogen ions from the acid react with the hydroxide ions from the alkali to produce water.
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, the equation the specification gives for the reaction of hydrogen ions with hydroxide ions.
A wide range indicator whose colour is matched to a chart to give an approximate pH.
A measured pH is used to classify a solution: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline.
A method of measuring the volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other, using a suitable indicator.
The graduated tube that delivers the solution added a little at a time, read to the nearest 0.05 cm³.
Apparatus that delivers an accurate fixed volume, used with a safety filler to place the alkali in the conical flask.
The moment when the indicator changes colour permanently, showing that the acid and alkali have exactly reacted.
Titres that agree within 0.10 cm³. The rough titre is discarded and the mean is taken from the concordant results.
Amount of substance in moles divided by volume in dm³; volumes in cm³ are divided by 1000 first.
Mass in grams per dm³ of solution; it equals the concentration in mol/dm³ multiplied by Mᵣ.
An acid that is completely ionised in aqueous solution. Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids are strong acids.
An acid that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution. Ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are weak acids.
The fraction of the acid molecules that have released their hydrogen ions. It is what strong and weak describe.
As pH falls by one unit the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10.
A small amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution. Dilute is about amount, not about ionisation.
A large amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution. A weak acid can still be concentrated.
Comparing solutions by pH: the lower the whole-number pH, the greater the hydrogen ion concentration, with pH 7 as neutral.

misconceptions.question: Copper is added to dilute sulfuric acid. Does it produce a salt and hydrogen?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only some metals react with dilute acids. Magnesium, zinc and iron do; copper does not, so nothing happens.
misconceptions.misconception: All metals react with acids, so every metal will fizz and give off hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is first met as 'acid + metal → salt + hydrogen', which reads like a rule for all metals, and the metals handed out in class are chosen because they react.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says acids react with some metals. A metal only releases hydrogen if it is more reactive than hydrogen; copper, silver and gold are not.

misconceptions.question: What are the products when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: A metal and an acid give a salt and water, like every other acid reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Salt and water is the first product pair students meet and it is repeated so often that it becomes the answer to any acid question.
misconceptions.correction: Sort the reactions by what the acid meets: metal gives hydrogen, base or alkali gives water, carbonate gives water and carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.question: Does carbon dioxide form when an acid reacts with a metal or a metal oxide?
misconceptions.correct: No. Carbon dioxide is only produced when the acid reacts with a carbonate.
misconceptions.misconception: Acid reactions fizz, and fizzing means carbon dioxide, so carbon dioxide is always a product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The carbonate reaction is memorable because of the vigorous fizzing, and the gas from an acid-metal reaction also looks like bubbles.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon must come from somewhere. Only a carbonate contains carbon, so only a carbonate can give carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.question: Which salt does hydrochloric acid produce?
misconceptions.correct: Chlorides, containing the Cl⁻ ion.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrochloric acid produces chlorates.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Chlorate sounds like a tidy '-ate' ending to match nitrate and sulfate, so students regularise the name.
misconceptions.correction: Chlorate, ClO₃⁻, contains oxygen and is not made by hydrochloric acid. Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides.

misconceptions.question: Which salt forms when iron reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Iron(II) chloride, FeCl₂.
misconceptions.misconception: Iron always forms the 3+ ion, so the product is iron(III) chloride.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Iron(III) compounds are met first in rusting, and the 3+ ion is the one students remember.
misconceptions.correction: Dilute acid takes iron only as far as Fe²⁺, so the salt is iron(II) chloride and two chloride ions balance the charge.

misconceptions.question: Balance: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂
misconceptions.correct: It is already balanced as written.
misconceptions.misconception: Extra numbers must be added, for example doubling the acid or writing the hydrogen as 2H.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students balance by changing whatever is nearest rather than counting atoms of every element on both sides.
misconceptions.correction: Count each element: 1 Zn, 2 H, 1 S and 4 O on both sides. Hydrogen gas is always H₂, never a lone H.

misconceptions.question: In Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, which species is oxidised?
misconceptions.correct: Zinc, because it loses two electrons to form Zn²⁺.
misconceptions.misconception: Zinc gains electrons, so zinc is reduced and the hydrogen ions are oxidised.
misconceptions.whyItArises: OIL RIG is memorised as a phrase but not attached to a picture, so the two halves get swapped under pressure.
misconceptions.correction: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain — of electrons. A metal atom becoming a positive ion must have lost electrons.

misconceptions.question: Which species is reduced when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: The hydrogen ions: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
misconceptions.misconception: The metal is reduced, because the metal is the reactive one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Reduced' is heard as 'used up' or 'made smaller', and it is the metal that visibly disappears.
misconceptions.correction: Reduction means gain of electrons. The metal loses electrons, so it is the hydrogen ions that are reduced.

misconceptions.question: Is Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ a redox reaction, given that no oxygen is involved?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Electrons are transferred from magnesium to hydrogen ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Without oxygen there can be no oxidation, so it is not redox.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxidation is introduced as gain of oxygen, and that first definition sticks.
misconceptions.correction: At Higher tier redox is defined by electron transfer. Gain and loss of oxygen is only one example of it.

misconceptions.question: Does hydrogen form when an acid is neutralised by an alkali or a metal oxide?
misconceptions.correct: No. Acid + alkali or base gives a salt and water only.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen is given off whenever an acid reacts, because acids contain hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The acid-metal reaction is done first and is the most visually striking, so hydrogen becomes the expected gas.
misconceptions.correction: The hydrogen ions from the acid end up in water when the acid meets a base or alkali. Hydrogen gas needs a metal to give up electrons.

misconceptions.question: What are the products of nitric acid and calcium carbonate?
misconceptions.correct: Calcium nitrate, water and carbon dioxide — three products.
misconceptions.misconception: Only a salt and water are formed, as with any other neutralisation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn 'acid + base → salt + water' as the neutralisation equation and apply it to carbonates too.
misconceptions.correction: A carbonate also supplies carbon and oxygen, so carbon dioxide is released as well; that is the fizzing that is seen.

misconceptions.question: Is copper(II) oxide an alkali?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a base, because it neutralises acid, but it does not dissolve in water.
misconceptions.misconception: Every base is an alkali, so any metal oxide or hydroxide can be called an alkali.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words are used side by side in lessons and both are 'the opposite of acid', so they are treated as synonyms.
misconceptions.correction: An alkali is a soluble base. If it does not dissolve to give a solution containing OH⁻ ions, it is a base only.

misconceptions.question: Which salt does nitric acid produce?
misconceptions.correct: Nitrates, containing the NO₃⁻ ion.
misconceptions.misconception: Nitric acid produces nitrides, or else nitrites.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three names sound almost identical and the endings are not connected to the actual ions.
misconceptions.correction: Nitride is N³⁻ and nitrite is NO₂⁻. Nitric acid, HNO₃, supplies the nitrate ion NO₃⁻.

misconceptions.question: Which salt does sulfuric acid produce?
misconceptions.correct: Sulfates, containing the SO₄²⁻ ion.
misconceptions.misconception: Sulfuric acid produces sulfides.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sulfide is the shorter, more familiar word, and the oxygen in the sulfate ion is easy to forget.
misconceptions.correction: Sulfide is S²⁻, made from sulfur alone. Sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, supplies the sulfate ion SO₄²⁻.

misconceptions.question: Sulfuric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide. Where does the sodium in the salt come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the alkali. The acid supplies only the sulfate ion.
misconceptions.misconception: The acid supplies both halves of the salt, so any acid with any base gives the same salt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The acid is the substance being 'used' in the reaction, so it is assumed to be the source of everything in the product.
misconceptions.correction: Split the salt in two: the positive ion comes from the base, alkali or carbonate, and the negative ion comes from the acid.

misconceptions.question: Ca²⁺ and NO₃⁻. What is the formula of calcium nitrate?
misconceptions.correct: Ca(NO₃)₂ — two nitrate ions balance one calcium ion.
misconceptions.misconception: The ions are simply written side by side, giving CaNO₃.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae are copied as symbol pairs without checking that the positive and negative charges cancel.
misconceptions.correction: Count the charge. 2+ must be cancelled by two 1− ions, so two nitrates are needed and brackets show that.

misconceptions.question: Is Zn₂(SO₄)₂ an acceptable formula for zinc sulfate?
misconceptions.correct: No. The ratio simplifies to ZnSO₄.
misconceptions.misconception: Any ratio that balances the charges will do, so it need not be simplified.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students cross over the charges mechanically and never check whether the subscripts share a common factor.
misconceptions.correction: A formula uses the simplest whole-number ratio of ions, so Zn₂(SO₄)₂ must be reduced to ZnSO₄.

misconceptions.question: Should the acid or the solid be in excess when preparing a soluble salt?
misconceptions.correct: The solid. It is added until no more reacts, so that all the acid is used up.
misconceptions.misconception: Excess acid should be left, because the acid is what makes the salt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The acid is seen as the active ingredient, so having more of it feels safer.
misconceptions.correction: Excess acid cannot be filtered off and would stay in the crystals. Excess solid can be filtered out, so the solid is the one to have spare.

misconceptions.question: After filtering the reaction mixture, which part contains the salt?
misconceptions.correct: The filtrate. The salt is dissolved and passes through the paper.
misconceptions.misconception: The salt is the residue collected on the filter paper.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Filtering is usually met as a way of collecting a solid product, so the solid left behind is assumed to be what you want.
misconceptions.correction: The salt made here is soluble, so it is in solution. The residue is the unreacted solid you are throwing away.

misconceptions.question: Can sodium hydroxide solution be used as the excess substance in this preparation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The method needs an insoluble solid that can be filtered off.
misconceptions.misconception: Any base will do, including a solution of an alkali.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are bases and both neutralise the acid, so the difference in solubility is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Excess alkali would stay dissolved and contaminate the salt. An insoluble oxide, hydroxide or carbonate can be filtered out.

misconceptions.question: How should the salt solution be evaporated?
misconceptions.correct: Gently, leaving the last of the water to evaporate slowly so crystals grow.
misconceptions.misconception: Boil it dry over a strong flame to get the salt quickly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Evaporating to dryness looks like the fastest route to a solid, and the crystallising step seems like waiting for nothing.
misconceptions.correction: Strong heating gives a powder and can decompose the salt or drive off water of crystallisation. Concentrate the solution, then leave it to crystallise.

misconceptions.question: How should the crystals be dried?
misconceptions.correct: Pat them between filter papers, or leave them in a warm place.
misconceptions.misconception: Rinse them with more acid, or heat them strongly, to clean and dry them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Washing is associated with purifying, and the acid is the liquid to hand.
misconceptions.correction: Acid would contaminate the sample and strong heating decomposes it. Drying is done gently, without adding anything.

misconceptions.question: Which heating is used for each stage of Required practical 1?
misconceptions.correct: A Bunsen burner warms the dilute acid; a water bath or electric heater evaporates the solution.
misconceptions.misconception: A Bunsen burner is used throughout, including for the evaporation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One heat source is expected for the whole experiment, and the Bunsen is the familiar one.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names a water bath or electric heater for the evaporation, because gentle heating protects the crystals.

misconceptions.question: Which ion do acids produce in aqueous solution?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen ions, H⁺.
misconceptions.misconception: Acids produce hydroxide ions, or negatively charged hydrogen ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two ions are learned as a pair and are easily swapped; the charge on H⁺ is also often written the wrong way.
misconceptions.correction: Acids produce H⁺, a positive ion. Alkalis produce OH⁻. The acid's own H⁺ is what makes the solution acidic.

misconceptions.question: Which ion is present in an alkaline solution?
misconceptions.correct: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkalis produce hydrogen ions, because their formulae contain hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium hydroxide contains an H in its formula, so hydrogen ions seem to be present.
misconceptions.correction: The H in OH⁻ is bonded to the oxygen within the hydroxide ion; it is not released as H⁺.

misconceptions.question: What is the range of the pH scale and what does it measure?
misconceptions.correct: It runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
misconceptions.misconception: It starts at 1, or stops at 7, or measures how strong an acid is by definition.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Classroom charts often start at 1, and 'strong acid' and 'low pH' are used loosely as if they meant the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: The scale is 0 to 14. pH measures acidity, which depends on hydrogen ion concentration and so on both strength and concentration.

misconceptions.question: Which gives a more precise pH: universal indicator or a pH probe?
misconceptions.correct: A pH probe. Universal indicator gives only an approximate value.
misconceptions.misconception: The indicator is more reliable because you can see the colour for yourself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour is direct evidence, and the probe is a black box that has to be trusted.
misconceptions.correction: Matching a colour to a chart gives a value to the nearest unit at best; a calibrated probe gives a numerical reading.

misconceptions.question: A solution has pH 2. Is it acidic or alkaline?
misconceptions.correct: Acidic. Solutions below pH 7 are acidic.
misconceptions.misconception: A low pH means weakly acidic or even alkaline, because the number is small.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A small number is read as 'a small amount of acid', so the direction of the scale is inverted.
misconceptions.correction: The scale runs the other way: the lower the pH, the greater the hydrogen ion concentration and the more acidic the solution.

misconceptions.question: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali.
misconceptions.correct: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
misconceptions.misconception: The formula or the numbers are altered, giving H₂O₂, or unequal numbers of ions on the two sides.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is recalled as a shape rather than counted, and H₂O₂ looks like a plausible product of two ions.
misconceptions.correction: One H⁺ and one OH⁻ contain two H, one O in total, which is exactly H₂O. Any coefficient must appear on both sides.

misconceptions.question: How precise is a pH measured with universal indicator?
misconceptions.correct: Approximate — to the nearest pH unit at best.
misconceptions.misconception: The colour chart gives an exact pH value.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The chart shows numbered colours, so it looks like a precise scale.
misconceptions.correction: Universal indicator is a wide range indicator: it gives an approximate pH. A pH probe is needed for a precise value.

misconceptions.question: Two solutions have pH 7 and pH 9. What does that tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The first is neutral; the second is alkaline.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that is not obviously acidic is neutral, and a neutral solution contains no ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutral is heard as 'nothing there', and pH 7 is associated with pure water.
misconceptions.correction: Only pH 7 is neutral. A neutral solution still contains ions — equal numbers of H⁺ and OH⁻.

misconceptions.question: Why is universal indicator not used in a titration?
misconceptions.correct: Its colour changes gradually through a range, so the end point cannot be judged sharply.
misconceptions.misconception: Universal indicator would work, since it shows the pH the whole way through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Showing more information seems better, and the pH is what the reaction is changing.
misconceptions.correction: A titration needs one sharp change at the end point. A single indicator such as phenolphthalein gives that; a gradual colour range does not.

misconceptions.question: Which apparatus measures the 25.0 cm³ of alkali placed in the flask?
misconceptions.correct: A pipette, used with a safety filler.
misconceptions.misconception: A measuring cylinder is close enough, or the burette can be used for both solutions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All three pieces of glassware measure volume, so they feel interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: A pipette delivers a fixed volume accurately; a measuring cylinder is far less precise. The burette is for the solution added gradually.

misconceptions.question: How is the burette prepared before filling?
misconceptions.correct: Rinse it with the solution it will hold, then fill and remove the air bubble below the tap.
misconceptions.misconception: Rinsing with water is enough, because water is clean.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rinsing is associated with cleaning, and water is the standard cleaning liquid.
misconceptions.correction: Water left in the burette dilutes the solution and changes the titre. Rinse with the solution being used.

misconceptions.question: Titres of 24.10, 23.55 and 23.60 cm³ are recorded. Which are used?
misconceptions.correct: The mean of 23.55 and 23.60, the two concordant results.
misconceptions.misconception: All three should be averaged, since more readings make a better mean.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Averaging everything is the general rule taught for repeat readings, and discarding data feels like cheating.
misconceptions.correction: The first titre is a rough one. Concordant titres agree within 0.10 cm³, and only those are averaged.

misconceptions.question: How is concentration in mol/dm³ calculated from moles and volume?
misconceptions.correct: Concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: Moles are multiplied by volume, or the two volumes in a titration are used the wrong way round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The triangle is memorised without meaning, so any arrangement of the three quantities looks equally likely.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration is an amount per unit volume, so it must be a division. Use the volume of the solution whose concentration you want.

misconceptions.question: A volume is given in cm³. What must be done before using it with mol/dm³?
misconceptions.correct: Divide by 1000 to convert to dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: The cm³ value is used as it stands, or is divided by 1000 twice.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The unit conversion is a separate step that is easy to skip, and once it is remembered it is sometimes applied again.
misconceptions.correction: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. Convert once, at the start, and check that the answer is a sensible size.

misconceptions.question: How is a concentration in mol/dm³ converted to g/dm³?
misconceptions.correct: Multiply by Mᵣ.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide by Mᵣ, or divide Mᵣ by the concentration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Moles and mass are linked by both multiplying and dividing in different problems, so the direction is guessed.
misconceptions.correction: Mass = moles × Mᵣ, so concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × Mᵣ.

misconceptions.question: What is the difference between a concentrated acid and a strong acid?
misconceptions.correct: Concentrated is about the amount dissolved per dm³; strong is about complete ionisation.
misconceptions.misconception: Concentrated and strong mean the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech a 'strong' drink is a concentrated one, and both words describe something powerful.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two ideas apart: concentration is how much acid is there; strength is what fraction of it has ionised.

misconceptions.question: What does calling an acid weak tell you?
misconceptions.correct: That it is only partially ionised in solution.
misconceptions.misconception: That it is dilute, so there is not much of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Weak is heard as 'watered down', which is the everyday meaning.
misconceptions.correction: Weak describes the degree of ionisation. A weak acid can be concentrated, and a strong acid can be dilute.

misconceptions.question: Is ethanoic acid completely ionised in water?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a weak acid and is only partially ionised.
misconceptions.misconception: All acids ionise completely; weak just means there is less of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ionisation is presented as what acids do, and partial ionisation is a harder idea to picture.
misconceptions.correction: In a weak acid only a small fraction of the molecules release their H⁺ at any time, so the hydrogen ion concentration is lower.

misconceptions.question: The pH falls from 5 to 3. By what factor does the hydrogen ion concentration change?
misconceptions.correct: It increases by a factor of 100.
misconceptions.misconception: It increases by a factor of 2, because the pH changed by 2.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The pH difference is treated as a multiplier on a linear scale.
misconceptions.correction: Each pH unit is a factor of 10, so two units is 10 × 10 = 100.

misconceptions.question: The pH falls by two units. Is that a tenfold change?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a hundredfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.
misconceptions.misconception: Any fall in pH means a factor of ten.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'one unit is ten times' is remembered, but it is applied once however many units change.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the factor of 10 once for each unit: two units gives 10², three units gives 10³.

misconceptions.question: Two acids have the same concentration. Which has the lower pH?
misconceptions.correct: The stronger acid, because it produces more hydrogen ions.
misconceptions.misconception: The weaker acid has the lower pH, because weak sounds like more acidic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Strength and pH are linked in the right way but the direction of the pH scale is inverted.
misconceptions.correction: More hydrogen ions means a lower pH. The stronger acid ionises more, so its pH is lower.

misconceptions.question: Can a weak acid be concentrated?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Weak and concentrated describe different things.
misconceptions.misconception: A weak acid must be dilute, and a concentrated acid must be strong.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The four words are learned as two opposite pairs and are then assumed to line up with each other.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration and strength vary independently: concentrated ethanoic acid is a concentrated weak acid.

misconceptions.question: Does the acid used change which salt is made?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, nitric acid nitrates and sulfuric acid sulfates.
misconceptions.misconception: Any acid gives the same salt, since the metal is what names it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The metal is written first in the salt's name, so it seems to be the part that matters.
misconceptions.correction: Both halves matter. The acid decides the second half of the name and the negative ion in the formula.

misconceptions.question: Which ion is common to all acids in aqueous solution?
misconceptions.correct: The hydrogen ion, H⁺.
misconceptions.misconception: Each acid produces the ion named in its own name, such as chloride from hydrochloric acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The negative ion is the one that appears in the salt, so it is the one students focus on.
misconceptions.correction: The negative ion differs from acid to acid; H⁺ is what makes all of them acids.

misconceptions.question: The pH falls from 5 to 3. How many factors of ten is that?
misconceptions.correct: Two, giving a factor of 100.
misconceptions.misconception: Three, because the values 5, 4 and 3 have been counted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting the numbers listed rather than the gaps between them is the same slip as counting fence posts instead of gaps.
misconceptions.correction: Subtract the pH values: 5 − 3 = 2 units, so the factor is 10² = 100.

misconceptions.question: Where does the metal ion in a salt come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the base, alkali or carbonate.
misconceptions.misconception: From the water formed in the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both products appear at the same time, so the source of each part of the salt is not tracked.
misconceptions.correction: Water is a separate product, made from H⁺ and OH⁻. The metal ion was in the base, alkali or carbonate all along.

misconceptions.question: Why is excess solid added to the acid?
misconceptions.correct: To make sure all of the acid is used up.
misconceptions.misconception: To speed the reaction up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: More reactant usually means a faster reaction, so that is the reason that comes to mind.
misconceptions.correction: The purpose is completeness, not rate: leftover solid proves that no acid remains to contaminate the salt.

misconceptions.question: Is any of the salt left in the residue on the filter paper?
misconceptions.correct: No. The salt is soluble, so all of it is in the filtrate.
misconceptions.misconception: The salt is shared between the residue and the filtrate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mixtures are imagined as being split roughly in half by any separation.
misconceptions.correction: Filtration separates by solubility, not by proportion. Only insoluble material stays on the paper.

misconceptions.question: How do crystals form from a salt solution?
misconceptions.correct: By removing water, so the solution becomes saturated.
misconceptions.misconception: By adding water until crystals appear.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Crystals are associated with liquids, so adding more liquid seems to help them form.
misconceptions.correction: Adding water makes the solution more dilute, so crystals are less likely. Evaporate water instead.

misconceptions.question: Does an alkaline solution contain hydrogen molecules?
misconceptions.correct: No. It contains hydroxide ions, OH⁻.
misconceptions.misconception: The H in OH⁻ means hydrogen gas is present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol H appears in the formula, and hydrogen gas is the H species students meet most often.
misconceptions.correction: The hydrogen in the hydroxide ion is bonded to oxygen. Hydrogen gas is H₂ and is not present in the solution.

misconceptions.question: What quantity does a titration determine?
misconceptions.correct: The volumes of acid and alkali that exactly react.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass of salt produced by the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The salt preparation practical is done first, where a solid product is collected and weighed.
misconceptions.correction: Titration is a volume measurement. No product is isolated during it.

misconceptions.question: What is the burette used for in a titration?
misconceptions.correct: To add one solution gradually and measure the volume delivered.
misconceptions.misconception: To measure the fixed volume placed in the conical flask.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The burette is the most prominent piece of apparatus, so it is assumed to do the important measuring.
misconceptions.correction: The fixed volume is measured with a pipette. The burette measures the variable volume added to reach the end point.

misconceptions.question: Why is universal indicator unsuitable for a titration?
misconceptions.correct: Because its colour changes gradually rather than at a single point.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the indicator reacts with the acid and is used up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Anything added to a reaction mixture is assumed to be a reactant.
misconceptions.correction: Indicators are present in tiny amounts and are not consumed. The problem is the gradual colour change.

misconceptions.question: Which titre should be used if the results differ?
misconceptions.correct: The mean of the concordant titres.
misconceptions.misconception: The largest titre, or any single reading chosen at will.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Picking one number avoids the work of deciding which results agree.
misconceptions.correction: Discard the rough titre, check which results agree within 0.10 cm³, and average those.

misconceptions.question: How many moles are in 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ acid?
misconceptions.correct: 0.00200 mol — volume in dm³ multiplied by concentration.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.0200 mol, the converted volume on its own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The conversion step feels like the whole calculation, so the multiplication is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: Converting the units is only the first step. Moles = concentration × volume in dm³.

misconceptions.question: How are the two volumes in a titration used?
misconceptions.correct: Each volume is used with its own solution: moles from one, concentration for the other.
misconceptions.misconception: The two volumes are subtracted, or averaged, to give a single number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two similar numbers in a question invite an arithmetic operation between them.
misconceptions.correction: The volumes belong to different solutions. Find moles from the known solution, then divide by the other solution's volume in dm³.

misconceptions.question: A solution is 0.0800 mol/dm³. What is its concentration in g/dm³?
misconceptions.correct: 3.2 g/dm³, found by multiplying by Mᵣ.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.08 g/dm³ — the same number with different units.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Changing units often means only relabelling, so the conversion factor is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Moles and grams are different quantities. Multiply the concentration in mol/dm³ by Mᵣ to get g/dm³.

mcqs.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a piece of magnesium ribbon. What are the products?

options.text: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas
options.rationale: Acids react with some metals to produce a salt and hydrogen; hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, so the salt is magnesium chloride.

options.text: Magnesium chloride and water
options.rationale: The student applies the acid + base pattern of salt and water to a metal, but a metal releases hydrogen instead.

options.text: Magnesium chlorate plus hydrogen
options.rationale: The gas is right but the salt is misnamed: hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, never chlorates.

options.text: Magnesium chloride, water and CO₂
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is attached to every acid reaction, but only a carbonate can supply the carbon.

mcqs.stem: Pieces of magnesium, zinc, iron and copper are each added to dilute sulfuric acid. Only the copper gives no bubbles. Why?

options.text: Copper does react, but far too slowly to spot
options.rationale: The student believes every metal reacts with acid, so a metal that appears not to react is assumed to be reacting slowly.

options.text: Copper is too unreactive to release hydrogen
options.rationale: Acids react with only some metals. Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so it cannot release hydrogen from the acid.

options.text: Copper only reacts with hydrochloric acid
options.rationale: The acid is blamed rather than the metal, but copper is unreactive towards both dilute acids.

options.text: Copper is a solid so acid cannot attack it
options.rationale: Magnesium, zinc and iron are solids too and all three react, so the state is not the reason.

mcqs.stem: Which equation correctly represents the reaction of zinc with dilute sulfuric acid?

options.text: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O
options.rationale: Water is written as the second product because salt and water is remembered as the rule for every acid.

options.text: Zn + 2H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + 2H₂
options.rationale: The acid is doubled to match a doubled hydrogen molecule, which leaves sulfur and oxygen unbalanced.

options.text: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂
options.rationale: Sulfuric acid produces sulfates and the hydrogen is released as H₂. The equation is balanced as written.

options.text: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H
options.rationale: Hydrogen is written as a single atom; the gas released is the diatomic molecule H₂, and the equation no longer balances.

mcqs.stem: Iron filings are warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which salt is formed?

options.text: Iron(III) chloride, FeCl₃
options.rationale: Iron is assumed always to form the 3+ ion because iron(III) compounds are met in rusting.

options.text: Iron(II) chlorate, Fe(ClO₃)₂
options.rationale: The chloride ion is confused with the chlorate ion; hydrochloric acid gives chlorides.

options.text: Iron(III) chloride, Fe₂Cl₆
options.rationale: The ratio has not been simplified, and the 3+ ion is used as well.

options.text: Iron(II) chloride, FeCl₂
options.rationale: Dilute acid takes iron only as far as the Fe²⁺ ion, and two chloride ions balance that charge, giving FeCl₂.

mcqs.stem: (HT) Why is the reaction between zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid described as a redox reaction?

options.text: Zinc gains electrons and hydrogen ions lose them
options.rationale: Oxidation and reduction are swapped; loss of electrons is oxidation, so it is the metal that loses.

options.text: Zinc atoms lose electrons and hydrogen ions gain them
options.rationale: Redox is defined by electron transfer: zinc is oxidised as it loses electrons and the hydrogen ions are reduced as they gain them.

options.text: No oxygen is involved, so it is not a redox change
options.rationale: Redox is limited to gain and loss of oxygen, but at Higher tier it is defined by electron transfer.

options.text: Zinc and the acid simply swap their ions over
options.rationale: This describes an exchange of partners with no electron transfer, which would not be redox.

mcqs.stem: (HT) In the reaction Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, which species is oxidised?

options.text: Hydrogen ions, as they lose electrons
options.rationale: The hydrogen ions gain electrons to become H₂, so they are reduced, not oxidised.

options.text: Chloride ions, as they change place
options.rationale: Chloride ions are spectator ions; they keep the same charge throughout the reaction.

options.text: Magnesium, as it loses two electrons
options.rationale: Each magnesium atom loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺, and loss of electrons is oxidation.

options.text: Magnesium, as it gains electrons
options.rationale: The right species is chosen but the definition is inverted; magnesium loses its outer electrons.

mcqs.stem: (HT) Which line shows the reduction step when iron reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, and names it correctly?

options.text: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻, the loss of electrons
options.rationale: This is the oxidation half equation: the iron loses electrons rather than gaining them.

options.text: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻, written in reverse
options.rationale: The right species is chosen but the change is written backwards, showing loss of electrons.

options.text: Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe, forming the iron metal
options.rationale: Iron ions are being reduced here, which is the opposite of what happens to the iron in this reaction.

options.text: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, a gain of electrons
options.rationale: The hydrogen ions gain electrons to form hydrogen molecules, and gain of electrons is reduction.

mcqs.stem: Copper(II) oxide is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid. What is produced?

options.text: Copper sulfate and water only
options.rationale: A metal oxide is a base, and acids are neutralised by bases to produce a salt and water only.

options.text: Copper sulfate, water and hydrogen
options.rationale: Hydrogen is added because the acid + metal pattern has been applied to a metal oxide.

options.text: Copper sulfate and carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide can only come from a carbonate; an oxide contains no carbon.

options.text: Copper sulfide and water vapour
options.rationale: Sulfuric acid produces sulfates, not sulfides; the sulfate ion is SO₄²⁻.

mcqs.stem: Calcium carbonate chips are dropped into dilute nitric acid and the mixture fizzes. What are the three products?

options.text: Calcium nitrate and water, no gas
options.rationale: The fizzing is ignored and the acid + base pattern of salt and water is used instead.

options.text: Calcium nitrate, water and hydrogen
options.rationale: The gas is assumed to be hydrogen because bubbles are associated with acid + metal reactions.

options.text: Calcium nitrate, water and carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Metal carbonates neutralise acids to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide; nitric acid produces nitrates.

options.text: Calcium nitrite, water and CO₂ gas
options.rationale: Nitric acid produces nitrates (NO₃⁻); nitrite (NO₂⁻) is a different ion.

mcqs.stem: Which substance is correctly described as an alkali?

options.text: Copper(II) oxide, which is an insoluble base
options.rationale: Every base is treated as an alkali, but copper(II) oxide does not dissolve, so it is a base only.

options.text: Copper hydroxide, which will not dissolve
options.rationale: Any hydroxide is assumed to be an alkali, but it must dissolve in water to be one.

options.text: Hydrochloric acid, which neutralises
options.rationale: An acid is the substance being neutralised by an alkali; it is not an alkali itself.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide, a soluble metal hydroxide
options.rationale: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, so a soluble metal hydroxide such as sodium hydroxide is an alkali.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the salts made by acids is correct?

options.text: Nitric acid produces nitrates
options.rationale: The acid used decides the salt: hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid nitrates and sulfuric acid sulfates.

options.text: Sulfuric acid produces sulfides
options.rationale: The sulfate ion SO₄²⁻ is shortened to sulfide S²⁻, losing the oxygen atoms.

options.text: Hydrochloric acid gives chlorates
options.rationale: Chlorate (ClO₃⁻) is confused with chloride (Cl⁻), the ion hydrochloric acid actually supplies.

options.text: Nitric acid yields nitrites
options.rationale: Nitrite (NO₂⁻) is confused with nitrate (NO₃⁻).

mcqs.stem: Which pair of reactants would produce the salt potassium sulfate, K₂SO₄?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid and potassium hydroxide
options.rationale: The metal is right, but hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, so this pair gives potassium chloride.

options.text: Sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide
options.rationale: The acid supplies the sulfate ion and the alkali supplies the potassium ions, giving K₂SO₄ and water.

options.text: Nitric acid and potassium hydroxide solution
options.rationale: Nitric acid produces nitrates, so this pair gives potassium nitrate rather than a sulfate.

options.text: Sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide solution
options.rationale: The acid is right, but the positive ion comes from the alkali, so this pair gives sodium sulfate.

mcqs.stem: In a reaction between an acid and a base, where does the positive ion in the salt come from?

options.text: From the acid that is being used
options.rationale: The acid is assumed to supply both parts of the salt, but it only supplies the negative ion.

options.text: From the water formed in the reaction
options.rationale: The salt is thought to be built out of the water product; water is a separate product of neutralisation.

options.text: From the indicator that has been added
options.rationale: An indicator only signals the end point and takes no part in forming the salt.

options.text: From the base, alkali or carbonate used
options.rationale: The acid supplies the negative ion of the salt and the base, alkali or carbonate supplies the positive metal ion.

mcqs.stem: Predict the products of the reaction between dilute hydrochloric acid and zinc oxide.

options.text: Zinc chloride and water only
options.rationale: Zinc oxide is a base, so it neutralises the acid to give a salt and water; hydrochloric acid gives a chloride.

options.text: Zinc chloride and hydrogen gas
options.rationale: The metal oxide is treated as a metal, so hydrogen is predicted in place of water.

options.text: Zinc chlorate plus water
options.rationale: Hydrochloric acid produces chlorides; chlorate is a different, oxygen-containing ion.

options.text: Zinc chloride and CO₂ gas
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is expected from every acid reaction, but zinc oxide contains no carbon.

mcqs.stem: Calcium ions are Ca²⁺ and nitrate ions are NO₃⁻. What is the formula of calcium nitrate?

options.text: CaNO₃
options.rationale: The ions are combined one to one, which leaves the formula with an overall positive charge.

options.text: Ca(NO₃)₂
options.rationale: Two nitrate ions are needed to balance the 2+ charge on one calcium ion, and the bracket shows that both are nitrate ions.

options.text: Ca₂(NO₃)₂
options.rationale: The ratio has not been simplified; two of each ion reduces to one calcium and two nitrates.

options.text: Ca(NO₃)(NO₃)
options.rationale: The two nitrate ions are written out separately instead of using a bracket and a subscript.

mcqs.stem: Zinc ions are Zn²⁺ and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of zinc sulfate?

options.text: Zn₂SO₄
options.rationale: The sulfate ion is treated as having a single negative charge, so two zinc ions are wrongly used.

options.text: Zn(SO₄)₂
options.rationale: Two sulfate ions are used, which would leave the formula with an overall negative charge.

options.text: ZnSO₄
options.rationale: The 2+ and 2− charges cancel one to one, so no extra subscripts are needed.

options.text: Zn₂(SO₄)₂
options.rationale: The ratio has not been simplified down to its simplest whole numbers.

mcqs.stem: When making a soluble salt, why is the insoluble solid added to the acid until no more reacts?

options.text: To be sure that all of the acid has been used up
options.rationale: Adding solid until some is left over guarantees that no acid remains in the solution to contaminate the salt.

options.text: To make the reaction happen much more quickly
options.rationale: Excess solid is thought to speed the reaction up; it is used to make sure the acid is completely used.

options.text: To leave some spare acid to help crystals form
options.rationale: Leftover acid is thought to be needed later, but it would contaminate the dry salt.

options.text: To dissolve the solid completely in the acid
options.rationale: The method relies on some solid not dissolving, so that it can be filtered off.

mcqs.stem: Which solid should be added to dilute sulfuric acid to prepare copper sulfate by this method?

options.text: Copper metal turnings
options.rationale: Every metal is assumed to react with acid, but copper does not react with dilute sulfuric acid.

options.text: Copper(II) oxide powder
options.rationale: Copper metal is too unreactive, but copper(II) oxide is an insoluble base that neutralises the acid.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide solution
options.rationale: A soluble alkali cannot be filtered off, so the excess could not be removed from the salt solution.

options.text: Solid copper sulfate
options.rationale: This is the product, not a reactant; adding it would not neutralise the acid.

mcqs.stem: After the excess solid has been filtered off, where is the salt?

options.text: Trapped in the residue left on the filter paper
options.rationale: Filtering is thought to collect the product, but the residue is the leftover insoluble solid.

options.text: Split evenly between the residue and the filtrate
options.rationale: The salt is thought to be shared between the two parts; a dissolved salt is entirely in the filtrate.

options.text: Dissolved in the filtrate that passes through
options.rationale: The salt is soluble, so it stays in solution and passes through the filter paper as the filtrate.

options.text: Lost as a gas while the mixture is filtered
options.rationale: No gas is produced at this stage, and the salt is not volatile.

mcqs.stem: Which sequence produces a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble base?

options.text: Filter the acid first, then add the solid oxide
options.rationale: There is nothing to filter before the reaction, and unreacted solid would still be present at the end.

options.text: Add excess acid, filter it, then crystallise
options.rationale: Leaving the acid in excess means the crystals would be contaminated with unreacted acid.

options.text: Add the solid, then boil the whole mixture dry
options.rationale: Without filtering, the unreacted solid stays behind, and boiling dry spoils the crystals.

options.text: Add excess solid, filter, then crystallise
options.rationale: The excess solid removes all the acid, filtering removes that excess, and crystallising the filtrate gives the solid salt.

mcqs.stem: How is a solution of a salt best turned into good crystals of the solid salt?

options.text: Boil the solution dry over a roaring flame
options.rationale: Evaporating to dryness quickly gives a powder and can decompose the salt rather than forming crystals.

options.text: Evaporate some water, then leave it to crystallise
options.rationale: Salt solutions can be crystallised: the solution is concentrated, then left so that crystals form slowly as the rest of the water evaporates.

options.text: Add more water until crystals begin to appear
options.rationale: Adding water makes the solution more dilute, so crystals are less likely to form, not more.

options.text: Filter the warm solution through paper twice
options.rationale: Filtration removes insoluble solids; it cannot separate a dissolved salt from its water.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 1, how is the salt solution evaporated once the excess solid has been filtered off?

options.text: With a roaring Bunsen flame under the dish
options.rationale: Direct strong heating is assumed to be quicker, but it decomposes the salt and gives a powder.

options.text: By filtering the solution through paper
options.rationale: Filtration cannot remove water from a solution; only evaporation can.

options.text: Using a water bath or an electric heater
options.rationale: The specification names a water bath or an electric heater for the evaporation step, giving gentle, controlled heating.

options.text: By adding a drying agent to the liquid
options.rationale: No drying agent is used in this practical, and it would contaminate the salt.

mcqs.stem: Which ion do all acids produce in aqueous solution?

options.text: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
options.rationale: The ion of alkalis is chosen; hydroxide ions make a solution alkaline, not acidic.

options.text: Chloride ions, Cl⁻
options.rationale: The ion is taken from the name of one acid, but H⁺ is the ion common to all of them.

options.text: Oxide ions, O²⁻
options.rationale: Oxide ions come from metal oxides acting as bases, not from acids in solution.

options.text: Hydrogen ions, H⁺
options.rationale: Acids produce hydrogen ions, H⁺, in aqueous solutions; this is what makes a solution acidic.

mcqs.stem: What do aqueous solutions of alkalis contain?

options.text: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
options.rationale: Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions, OH⁻, which is why they neutralise acids.

options.text: The hydrogen ions, H⁺
options.rationale: The ion produced by acids is chosen; alkalis supply hydroxide ions instead.

options.text: Hydrogen molecules, H₂
options.rationale: The H in OH⁻ is read as hydrogen gas, but no hydrogen molecules are present in an alkali.

options.text: Water molecules only
options.rationale: Pure water is neutral; an alkaline solution must contain hydroxide ions as well.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the pH scale is correct?

options.text: It runs from 1 to 14 and measures the acid strength
options.rationale: The scale is remembered as starting at 1, and pH is treated as a direct measure of strength.

options.text: It runs from 0 to 7 for acids and no further
options.rationale: Only the acidic part of the scale is remembered, leaving no values for alkaline solutions.

options.text: It runs from 0 to 14 and measures acidity or alkalinity
options.rationale: The pH scale, from 0 to 14, is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution.

options.text: It runs from 0 to 14 and measures concentration
options.rationale: The range is right, but pH measures acidity, not the amount of acid dissolved.

mcqs.stem: Four solutions have pH values of 2, 7, 9 and 13. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The solution at pH 2 must be alkaline and pH 13 acidic
options.rationale: The scale is read the wrong way round, so a low pH is taken to mean alkaline.

options.text: Only the solution at pH 7 contains any ions
options.rationale: Neutral is taken to mean that nothing is dissolved, but all four solutions contain ions.

options.text: The solutions at pH 9 and pH 13 are both neutral
options.rationale: Any value that is not clearly acidic is treated as neutral; only pH 7 is neutral.

options.text: The solution at pH 2 is acidic and pH 13 is alkaline
options.rationale: Solutions with a pH below 7 are acidic and those above 7 are alkaline, so pH 2 is acidic and pH 13 alkaline.

mcqs.stem: Which equation represents the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali?

options.text: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
options.rationale: In neutralisation between an acid and an alkali, hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to produce water.

options.text: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O₂
options.rationale: The formula of water is written as hydrogen peroxide; one H⁺ and one OH⁻ give H₂O.

options.text: 2H⁺ + 2OH⁻ → H₂O
options.rationale: The numbers on each side no longer match: two of each ion would give two water molecules.

options.text: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂
options.rationale: Hydrogen gas is expected from every acid reaction, but neutralisation by an alkali produces water.

mcqs.stem: A few drops of universal indicator are added to a solution and the colour is matched to a chart. What does this give?

options.text: An exact pH value, correct to two decimal places
options.rationale: A colour chart is read as if it were a digital display; a pH probe is needed for a precise value.

options.text: An approximate value for the solution's pH
options.rationale: Universal indicator, a wide range indicator, gives an approximate pH when its colour is matched to a chart.

options.text: The concentration of the acid in mol per dm³
options.rationale: Indicator colour responds to acidity, not to the amount of acid measured out.

options.text: The volume of alkali needed for neutralisation
options.rationale: That volume is found by titration, not by a single colour match.

mcqs.stem: What is measured in a titration between an acid and an alkali?

options.text: The mass of salt made when they are mixed
options.rationale: The titration is confused with salt preparation, where the product is collected and weighed.

options.text: The temperature rise during the reaction
options.rationale: A temperature change does accompany neutralisation, but it is not what a titration measures.

options.text: The exact pH at every stage of the reaction
options.rationale: A titration uses one indicator to spot the end point rather than tracking pH throughout.

options.text: The volumes of the solutions that react together
options.rationale: Titration measures the volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other, using a suitable indicator.

mcqs.stem: In a titration, how should the 25.0 cm³ of alkali be measured into the conical flask?

options.text: With a pipette and a safety filler
options.rationale: A pipette delivers an accurate, fixed volume of alkali into the flask, and a filler is used instead of mouth suction.

options.text: With a measuring cylinder poured in
options.rationale: A measuring cylinder is far less precise, so the reacting volume would not be accurate.

options.text: From the burette holding the acid
options.rationale: The burette holds the solution added a little at a time; it does not deliver the fixed volume in the flask.

options.text: By weighing it out on a balance
options.rationale: A titration compares volumes, and a balance gives mass rather than volume.

mcqs.stem: Why is a single indicator such as phenolphthalein used in a titration rather than universal indicator?

options.text: Universal indicator changes through many colours
options.rationale: True, but the reason matters: that gradual range of colours is exactly what makes the end point hard to judge.

options.text: It changes colour sharply at the end point
options.rationale: A single indicator gives one sudden colour change, so the end point can be judged to the nearest drop.

options.text: Universal indicator reacts with the acid used
options.rationale: Indicators are not used up by the acid; the problem is the gradual colour change.

options.text: It makes the neutralisation happen faster
options.rationale: An indicator does not affect the rate of the reaction between acid and alkali.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 2, a student records titres of 24.10, 23.55 and 23.60 cm³. What should be done next?

options.text: Take the mean of all three titres recorded
options.rationale: Every reading is averaged, including the rough one, which drags the mean away from the true value.

options.text: Use the largest titre, because it is safest
options.rationale: A single titre is picked with no reason to prefer it; the concordant results are the reliable ones.

options.text: Average the two concordant titres only
options.rationale: The rough first titre is discarded and the mean is taken from the titres that agree within 0.10 cm³.

options.text: Repeat until the titres are all identical
options.rationale: Identical titres are not expected; results within 0.10 cm³ are treated as concordant.

mcqs.stem: (HT) How many moles are there in 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³?

options.rationale: The volume in dm³ is 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0200 dm³, so moles = 0.0200 × 0.100 = 0.00200 mol.

options.text: 2.00 mol
options.rationale: The volume is used in cm³ without converting to dm³, making the answer 1000 times too large.
Only the volume has been converted; the concentration has been left out of the calculation.

options.text: 200 mol
options.rationale: The volume has been divided by the concentration instead of multiplied, with no unit conversion.

mcqs.stem: (HT) 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, reacting 1:1. What is the concentration of the alkali?

options.text: 0.00800 mol/dm³
options.rationale: A conversion has been made twice, so the answer is ten times too small.

options.text: 0.0800 mol/dm³
options.rationale: Moles of acid = 0.0200 × 0.100 = 0.00200 mol, so moles of alkali = 0.00200 mol and 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol/dm³.

options.text: 0.125 mol/dm³
options.rationale: The volumes have been used the wrong way round, dividing by the acid volume instead of the alkali volume.

options.text: 0.05 mol/dm³
options.rationale: The two volumes have been subtracted or averaged rather than used with the number of moles.

mcqs.stem: (HT) A sodium hydroxide solution has a concentration of 0.0800 mol/dm³. What is this in g/dm³? (Mᵣ of NaOH = 40)

options.text: 0.002 g/dm³
options.rationale: The concentration has been divided by Mᵣ instead of being multiplied by it.

options.text: 0.08 g/dm³
options.rationale: The number has simply been copied across with new units; it must be multiplied by Mᵣ.

options.text: 3.2 g/dm³
options.rationale: Concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × Mᵣ = 0.0800 × 40 = 3.2 g/dm³.

options.text: 32 g/dm³
options.rationale: The multiplication has been done with 0.8 rather than 0.0800, moving the decimal point.

mcqs.stem: (HT) What does it mean to say that hydrochloric acid is a strong acid?

options.text: It contains a large amount of acid in each dm³
options.rationale: Strength is confused with concentration, which is about the amount of substance in a given volume.

options.text: It is only partly ionised in aqueous solution
options.rationale: This is the definition of a weak acid; a strong acid ionises completely.

options.text: It will react with every metal that is added to it
options.rationale: Strength describes ionisation, not which metals react; copper still does not react with it.

options.text: It is completely ionised in aqueous solution
options.rationale: A strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution, so every acid molecule releases its hydrogen ion.

mcqs.stem: (HT) Which set contains only weak acids?

options.text: Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids
options.rationale: These are the three strong acids, all of which are completely ionised in solution.

options.text: Ethanoic acid, citric acid and carbonic acid
options.rationale: Ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are the weak acids named in the specification; each is only partially ionised.

options.text: Ethanoic acid, nitric and sulfuric acids
options.rationale: Only the first is weak; nitric and sulfuric acids ionise completely.

options.text: Citric acid, carbonic acid and nitric acid
options.rationale: Nitric acid is a strong acid, so this set is not made up of weak acids only.

mcqs.stem: (HT) A bottle is labelled 'concentrated ethanoic acid'. What does the word concentrated tell you?

options.text: The ethanoic acid in it is completely ionised
options.rationale: Concentrated is read as meaning strong, but the degree of ionisation does not change with concentration.

options.text: Only a small fraction of the acid molecules ionise
options.rationale: This describes weak, which ethanoic acid is, but it is not what the word concentrated tells you.

options.text: A large amount of acid is dissolved in each dm³
options.rationale: Concentrated describes the amount of substance dissolved in a given volume; ethanoic acid is still a weak acid.

options.text: It cannot be a weak acid when concentrated
options.rationale: Weak and concentrated are independent: a weak acid can be made as concentrated as you like.

mcqs.stem: (HT) The pH of a solution falls from 5 to 3. How does the hydrogen ion concentration change?

options.text: It increases by a factor of 2
options.rationale: The change in the pH number is used directly as the factor, ignoring the factor of 10 per unit.

options.text: It increases by a factor of 1000
options.rationale: The pH values 5, 4 and 3 have been counted as three steps; the pH has fallen by only two units.

options.text: It increases by a factor of ten only
options.rationale: One step of ten has been counted, but the pH has fallen by two units.

options.text: It increases by a factor of 100
options.rationale: Each fall of one pH unit multiplies the hydrogen ion concentration by 10, so a fall of two units multiplies it by 100.

mcqs.stem: (HT) Equal concentrations of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid are compared. Which has the lower pH, and why?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid, as it fully ionises
options.rationale: For a given concentration, the stronger acid produces more hydrogen ions, so it has the lower pH.

options.text: Ethanoic acid, as it ionises only partly
options.rationale: Partial ionisation gives fewer hydrogen ions, so the pH is higher, not lower.

options.text: Hydrochloric acid, as it is more concentrated
options.rationale: The right acid is chosen for the wrong reason: the two concentrations are stated to be equal.

options.text: Neither, as their concentrations are equal
options.rationale: Equal concentration does not mean an equal hydrogen ion concentration, because the degree of ionisation differs.

mcqs.stem: (HT) Solution X has pH 4 and solution Y has pH 7. What can be said about their hydrogen ion concentrations?

options.text: X has just 3 times the hydrogen ion concentration of Y
options.rationale: The difference in pH is used as a simple multiplier instead of as a power of ten.

options.text: Y has the higher hydrogen ion concentration here
options.rationale: A higher pH means fewer hydrogen ions, so Y has the lower concentration.

options.text: X has 1000 times the hydrogen ion concentration of Y
options.rationale: Three pH units below neutral means the hydrogen ion concentration is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 times greater.

options.text: Both are neutral, so the two values must match
options.rationale: Only pH 7 is neutral; solution X at pH 4 is acidic and has far more hydrogen ions.
